paragraphs.text: Hyposulfatemia with skeletal dysplasia (HSSD) is an autosomal recessive disorder in which loss of the renal and intestinal sodium-sulfate cotransporter SLC13A1 causes increased urinary sulfate excretion and low plasma sulfate. Affected children have skeletal abnormalities that can include spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia in early childhood, proportionate short stature and scoliosis. Some radiologic abnormalities have improved with age. Neurodevelopmental features, including autistic features, have been reported in some patients (van de Kamp et al., 2023; Tise et al., 2025).

paragraphs.text: van de Kamp et al. (2023) reported a Dutch boy, the only child of nonconsanguineous parents, who presented at 4 months of age with enlarged knees that could not fully extend. His length (-0.5 SDS) and head circumference (+0.5 SDS) were normal. A skeletal survey at 6 months showed generalized abnormalities: ovoid vertebral bodies, spiky widening of the metaphyses, irregular tarsal bones, slight flaring of the ribs and somewhat small epiphyses, which were more noticeable at 4 years. The skull and pelvis were normal. Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 were also normal. His growth was normal, and his only complaints were a slightly abnormal gait and an inability to run easily. He had a forearm fracture at 8 years, which healed well. The radiologic abnormalities improved, and by 11 years only flattening of the cervical vertebral bodies and irregular lumbar vertebral endplates remained. At 12 years he had enlarged knees and elbows, reduced movement in the lumbar spine and knees, winged scapulae, hypermobile fingers and flat feet. His height was normal (+1 SDS), but his trunk was relatively short, with a sitting height/height ratio of -2.0 SDS. On DEXA at 13 years, bone mineral density Z-scores were 0.2 in the lumbar spine and -2.1 in the proximal femur. Puberty began at 11.5 years. His cognitive development was above average, but he had autistic features that often led to panic attacks and school absenteeism. He also had cystic fibrosis, an incidental finding on exome sequencing.

paragraphs.text: Tise et al. (2025) reported 5 children from 4 families who were identified through exome or genome sequencing and GeneMatcher. All of them presented with concern for short stature and had scoliosis and/or skeletal dysplasia. Proband 1 was a 3-year-old boy of European ancestry born to nonconsanguineous parents. He presented at 2 years with increasing hip pain and had a history of bilateral developmental hip dysplasia that required bracing until 9 months of age. He had proportionate short stature (z-score below -2 SD) and mild dysmorphic facial features: bilateral epicanthal folds, a flattened nasal bridge, and a short, anteverted nose. He also had tapered fingers and deep-set nails of the halluces. Serial pelvic x-rays from 9 months showed delayed, stippled femoral ossification consistent with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. A spine x-ray at 2 years showed mild anterior beaking of the lumbar vertebrae.

paragraphs.text: Probands 3 (male) and 4 (female) of Tise et al. (2025) were fraternal twins conceived by in vitro fertilization and born at 34 weeks' gestation to nonconsanguineous parents. In proband 3, x-rays taken at 10 months for pectus carinatum showed abnormal vertebrae. His skeletal surveys showed exaggerated thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis, anterior beaking of thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies, short and broad femoral necks, and flaring of the femoral and tibial metaphyses. These findings were consistent with spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD) and were interpreted as most consistent with Kniest dysplasia. He had a 12-degree thoracic curve at 4 years, which progressed to S-shaped scoliosis with a 28-degree thoracic curve by 13 years. His other history included a type 1 Chiari malformation, an atrial septal defect, idiopathic thrombocytopenia and strabismus. Proband 4 had skeletal surveys at 14 months and 2 years showing ovoid vertebrae with anterior wedging, broad and short femoral necks, and widened metaphyses of the tubular bones, also consistent with SEMD. She had broad thumbs, 2-3 toe syndactyly, and short, broad halluces. At 10 years their heights were 129.6 cm (5th percentile) and 134.4 cm (20th percentile), respectively. Urine glycosaminoglycan analysis was normal in proband 3, and COL2A1 sequencing found no variants in either twin.

paragraphs.text: Proband 5 of Tise et al. (2025) was a boy, the only child of nonconsanguineous parents, who presented at 14 years with concern for scoliosis. He had proportionate short stature (157.3 cm, z = -2.13). Radiographs showed a 42-degree right thoracic curve and a 26-degree left thoracic curve, reduced vertebral body height of multiple mid and lower thoracic vertebrae, and concave endplates. He also had mild to moderate neurocognitive impairment, Asperger disorder and anxiety disorders. Tise et al. (2025) noted that a previously reported child homozygous for R12X had autistic features, and that more patients would be needed to determine whether SLC13A1 loss-of-function variants are associated with a neurodevelopmental phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In the patient reported by van de Kamp et al. (2023), plasma sulfate was severely reduced, which the authors described as a reduction of more than 80%. Plasma sulfate in both heterozygous parents was also below the control range. The patient's fractional sulfate excretion was close to 100% (reference range, 13% to 34%), consistent with complete loss of renal sulfate reabsorption. His mother's fractional sulfate excretion was 45%. Serum cholesterol sulfate was reduced (443 ng/ml; reference range 500-1236 ng/ml), whereas other serum steroid sulfates were within the reference range. The percentage of chondroitin sulfate disaccharides in urinary glycosaminoglycans did not differ significantly between the patient, his parents and controls.

paragraphs.text: In 5 children from 4 families with HSSD, Tise et al. (2025) identified homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC13A1 gene by exome or genome sequencing. Proband 1 was compound heterozygous for R12X, inherited from his father, and a c.1343G-A transition resulting in a gly448-to-asp (G448D) substitution, inherited from his mother. Proband 2 was homozygous for a c.1744T-C transition resulting in a tyr582-to-his (Y582H) substitution, which was found by a targeted search of SLC13A1 after trio genome sequencing had not identified a cause in a known disease gene. The twin probands 3 and 4 were compound heterozygous for a c.1547T-C transition resulting in a leu516-to-pro (L516P) substitution and a c.144G-A transition resulting in a trp48-to-ter (W48X) substitution. The text states that L516P was paternal and W48X maternal, whereas Table 1 assigns them the other way. Proband 5 was homozygous for W48X. The 4 missense variants tested in MDCK cells, R237C, G448D, L516P and Y582H, all caused complete loss of [35S]-sulfate transport activity. Plasma membrane expression of these variants was similar to that of wildtype.

paragraphs.text: van de Kamp et al. (2023) gave their patient intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) while he was on a protein-restricted diet. The dose was a bolus of 133 mg/kg over 60 minutes, followed by 133 mg/kg over 8 hours. Plasma sulfate normalized after the bolus and during the maintenance infusion but returned to baseline 15 hours after the infusion stopped. The patient developed erythema during the bolus, which resolved after intravenous clemastine. Because of a possible increased risk of hepatotoxicity, he was strongly advised to avoid acetaminophen. Tise et al. (2025) also advised caution in giving acetaminophen and other drugs metabolized by sulfation to individuals with biallelic SLC13A1 loss-of-function variants.

paragraphs.text: In fraternal twins with HSSD (probands 3 and 4), Tise et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC13A1 gene: a c.1547T-C transition, resulting in a leu516-to-pro (L516P) substitution, and the W48X mutation. The text gives L516P as paternally inherited, whereas Table 1 lists it as maternal. In MDCK cells, the L516P variant caused complete loss of [35S]-sulfate transport activity.

agent.process_note: I read both full texts in full: van de Kamp et al. (2023), a single Dutch patient homozygous for R12X, and Tise et al. (2025), 5 children from 4 families. I checked the variant notations and other details against the texts, and used Grep to check the exact characters in quoted spans. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so I gave no gene MIM number. The chromosome location (7q31) comes from van de Kamp et al.'s description of the region of homozygosity. The papers disagree with themselves in two places, and I reported both. In Tise et al., the twins' parental origin of L516P and W48X differs between the text and Table 1. Proband 2's fractional excretion index is 0.38 in the text but 0.038 in Table 1. I did not list R237C as an allelic variant, because Tise et al. tested it functionally but did not assign it to any proband. I left out the animal-model data because they are only background citations in both papers.
